analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal mandate requiring transportation fuel to contain renewable ethanol.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the federal renewable fuel mandate never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires refiners to blend a minimum amount of renewable fuel, mainly ethanol made from corn, into gasoline and diesel. This bill would erase that requirement entirely, leaving refiners free to sell fuel with no renewable content. It was introduced by a Florida Republican with ten Republican cosponsors, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil refiners and petroleum marketers would gain the most: they would no longer have to comply with blending quotas or buy compliance credits to meet them. Drivers could see modestly lower fuel prices if refiners pass the savings along. Environmental groups and climate advocates have also long argued the ethanol mandate does more harm than good.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 211(o) of the Clean Air Act, eliminating the EPA's Renewable Fuel Standard program and its minimum renewable fuel volumes [S2] [S3].
Makes conforming changes to the Clean Air Act and the Petroleum Marketing Practices Act so that fuel regulations revert to their pre-mandate state [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corn and soybean farmers and the ethanol and biodiesel industries would lose a federally guaranteed market for their product. Removing the mandate would likely increase petroleum use and greenhouse gas emissions, a cost spread across everyone. Rural communities built around ethanol plants would bear concentrated losses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corn and soybean farmers, ethanol producers

drawbacks.text: Repeal would end the only federal requirement that transportation fuel contain renewable fuel, eliminating the main guaranteed demand for ethanol and biodiesel [S2].
With no blending mandate, refiners would be free to sell purely petroleum-based fuel, which would mean more oil consumption and higher emissions than under the current program [S2].
The bill contains no transition plan or replacement policy for the renewable fuel volumes, farm income, and rural jobs that currently depend on the mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Repealing the mandate would relieve refiners of a real compliance cost and might trim fuel prices slightly, and many economists across the political spectrum dislike blending mandates as market distortions. But the bill removes the mandate without replacing it, so the immediate losers would be farm-state producers and the environment, while the gains to consumers depend on refiners voluntarily passing savings along. As drafted, the costs land on identifiable groups and the environment while the benefits are diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, never received a hearing or markup, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Francis Rooney of Florida introduced the bill on June 21, 2019, joined by seven original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on June 21, 2019, and to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change three days later [S5].
The bill ended with 10 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action was ever recorded; the bill's last action was the subcommittee referral [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ethanol producers and corn farmers kept their federally guaranteed share of the fuel market, and the EPA's blending requirements stayed in place. Refiners continue paying compliance costs they wanted erased. For drivers and the climate, little changed either way.

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Renewable Fuel Standard and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 10 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill; no Democrat signed on.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote; it sat in subcommittee from June 2019 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat supported it; the bill then died in a committee controlled by Democrats without any recorded vote on the merits.

industries.note: Repeal would end refiners' obligation to blend renewable fuel and buy compliance credits, a cost they pass into fuel prices. Drivers might see slightly cheaper gasoline, but cheaper fuel would come from more petroleum use, not less.

The mandate guarantees these producers a required share of the national fuel supply; repeal would strip that away. The mandate currently supports rural jobs and farm income but is sustained through requirements on fuel rather than voluntary demand.
Farmers supply the corn and soybean feedstocks for mandated renewable fuel. Repeal would cut demand for their crops with no replacement program in the bill.
